marble.name: Odd and even numbers
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.prompt: If you give you a number like 37 or 84, can they quickly tell you whether it's odd or even — and explain how they know?

cluster.summary: Your child is being introduced to multiplication and division as ways of working with equal groups — understanding multiplication as repeated addition and division as sharing equally.

misconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.
representations: Two equal rows / the 2s array (even = two equal groups)
Ten-frame (full pairs vs one lonely counter)
Hundred square with even numbers shaded (alternating columns)
authoredAnswer: 7 is odd, 8 is even. A child reasoning correctly pairs the counters up (or splits into two equal groups): 8 makes 4 pairs with none left over, so it is even; 7 makes 3 pairs with one left over, so it is odd — even means it can be shared into two equal groups (or all paired) with nothing left, odd leaves one.
probe: Give the child 6 counters (even) and ask them to predict, before touching them, whether adding ONE more counter will keep it even or make it odd — and to say why. wrongAnswers.revealedBy: child gives the right label but, asked to show it, cannot make the pairs relevant or says 'because it just is / because it ends in 8'
wrongAnswers.fix: do NOT accept the digit rule as proof — have the child pair the counters physically and name 'even = everyone has a partner, odd = one left alone'; connect it back to why the digits work only after the pairing meaning is secure.

wrongAnswers.wrong: 7 is even (I can make two groups: 3 and 4)
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: child divides 7 into two unequal piles and declares it even 'because there are two groups'
wrongAnswers.fix: insist the two groups match one-to-one; line the piles up side by side so the leftover in 7 is visibly unpaired.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: child hesitates or guesses on two-digit numbers, treating the property as tied to size not structure
wrongAnswers.fix: show that only the pairing of the LAST counter matters; group in tens (always even) and check the ones, so the rule scales.

before.name: Division as equal sharing
before.reason: Odd/even is about whether a number can be divided into 2 equal groups

before.name: Counting in 2s
before.reason: Even numbers connect to counting in 2s
